predecessors.name: rassids
predecessors.text: Haraz and, from 1063, Sana'a, held by the Zaydi Rassids

predecessors.name: Najahid dynasty
predecessors.text: Zabid and the Tihama, taken in 1062

successors.name: Zurayid dynasty
successors.text: Dhu Jibla, at-Ta'kar, Ibb and Habb, which Muhammad bin Saba gained 'after marrying the last Sulayhid queen' (undated)

ledger.x: 1047: Ali al-Sulayhi founds the Sulayhid dynasty in the Haraz mountains.
1062: the Sulayhids take Zabid and the Tihama from the Najahids.
1063: the rest of Yemen falls to Ali.
1064: Mecca takes a Sulayhid client king.
1067: the Najahids are back in Zabid.
1067: Sulayhid influence at Mecca ends with Ali's death.
1083: the Zurayid brothers are set over Aden.
1083: the Ma'nid tributary at Aden is replaced by the Zurayids.
1087: Queen Arwa moves the capital from Sana'a to Jibla.
1087: the Najahids come back to Zabid.
By 1089 the Sulayhids no longer hold Zabid: Jayyash's undated return and Fatiq's accession in 1089.
1110: Aden slips out of Sulayhid tutelage.
1138: Queen Arwa dies and the Sulayhid dynasty ends.

wars.name: Sulayhid conquest of Yemen
wars.outcome: Ali al-Sulayhi rose in Haraz in 1047, took Zabid and the Tihama in 1062, forced Aden to pay tribute (1062) and held Sana'a from 1063, 'conquered the whole of Yemen in 1062' on the Sulayhid page.

wars.name: Sulayhid campaign in the Hejaz
wars.outcome: Ali moved into the Hejaz in late 1063, took Mecca by 1064, installed a client king and had the Fatimids named in the khutba.

wars.name: Sulayhid-Najahid wars
wars.outcome: The Najahids killed Ali on the pilgrimage road (1066 or 1067) and held Zabid; al-Mukarram captured Zabid and Asma in 1082 and al-Ahwal fled to Dahlak; Said al-Ahwal returned to Zabid in 1087 and was killed the same year by al-Mukarram; Jayyash returned to…

wars.name: Sulayhid campaign against Zabid (1110)
wars.outcome: The Sulayhid leader al-Mufaddal besieged Zabid with the Zurayid brothers, who were both killed in the siege; the city held.

certainty.note: No boundary line appears on the pages opened; the highlands, the Tihama and Aden are named places, and the peak extent is 'most of historical Yemen'.
